questionStem: A 32-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 2, comes to the physician for her first prenatal visit. Her last menstrual period was 17 weeks ago. Examination shows a uterine fundus that is palpated midway between the pubic symphysis and umbilicus . Her serum a-fetoprotein concentration is 2.6 multiples of the median . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Repeat measurement of serum a-fetoprotein concentration

correctExplanation: Ultrasonography to evaluate the fetus is the most appropriate next step with an increased a-fetoprotein (AFP) concentration in the maternal serum. The most common causes of increased AFP include an inaccurate gestational date, multiple gestations, abdominal wall defects (eg, gastroschisis, omphalocele), and neural tube defects (eg, anencephaly, spina bifida). Ultrasonography would allow the clinician to better delineate the gestational age of the fetus and to rule out multiple gestations. It would also identify any abdominal wall or neural tube defects. Amniocentesis can also be performed after ultrasonography to assess for amniotic fluid acetylcholinesterase, which would further indicate an underlying neural tube defect.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Repeat measurement of serum a-fetoprotein concentration (Choice A) could be considered if there was concern for a false positive result. Given the patient's result of an AFP concentration that is 2.6 multiples of the median, a false positive is unlikely. Serum studies for fetal erythrocytes (Choice B) if taken from the mother, would be collected to assess for mixing of maternal and fetal blood, of which there is no clinical evidence based on increased AFP alone. Testing for fetal anemia requires a fetal blood sample from the umbilical cord, which is invasive and risks the pregnancy. Less invasive measures such as ultrasonography should first be employed, when there is no suspicion of fetal anemia or maternal-fetal blood mixing. Amniocentesis (Choice D) is an invasive sampling of amniotic fluid through the abdominal wall, usually performed at 15-20 weeks' gestation. It may be considered after ultrasonography to further assess the presence of a neural tube defect through detecting the presence of amniotic fluid acetylcholinesterase. However, ultrasonography is a better initial diagnostic examination as amniocentesis is invasive and can result in complications such as fetal-maternal hemorrhage, premature rupture of membranes, and chorioamnionitis. Pregnancy termination (Choice E) is a highly individualized decision. In this case, determining the cause of increased AFP concentration would be important in determining whether pregnancy termination is a viable next step, especially given the possibility of a gestational dating error. Educational Objective: Common causes of increased a-fetoprotein concentration in maternal serum are an inaccurate gestational date, multiple gestations, and abdominal wall or neural tube defects. Initial evaluation is performed with ultrasonography to evaluate the accuracy of the gestational date, number of fetuses, and presence of abdominal wall or neural tube abnormalities. " , ~ F' r ,

questionStem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because she has never had a menstrual period . She also has had moderate lower abdominal pain during the past 5 months . She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 52 kg (115 lb); BMI is 20 kg/m 2• Breast development is Tanner stage 4. Examination shows coarse pubic and axillary hair. The external genitalia appear normal. The vaginal canal cannot be visualized . Rectal examination shows an anterior tender , central mass. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: lmperforate hymen is a common, congenital disorder wherein the hymenal opening is absent, leading to the obstruction of the vaginal canal and preventing the excretion of menstrual blood. lmperforate hymen presents with amenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, and a bulging pelvic mass in an adolescent with otherwise normal sexual development. Significant accumulation of menstrual blood products may give the bulging hymen a blue appearance and may be palpated through the rectum, a condition known as hematocolpos. Diagnosis is made by ultrasonography. lmperforate hymen is treated with surgical hymenotomy and evacuation of the accumulated blood.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Androgen insensitivity syndrome (Choice A) may present with primary amenorrhea and a blind vaginal pouch. It occurs in patients with an XY karyotype who possess an inactivating mutation of the androgen receptor. While patients have a female external phenotype, karyotyping shows an XY genotype, and ultrasonography shows testes and the absence of a uterus, fallopian tubes, and the upper third of the vaginal canal. Axillary and pubic hair is sparse or absent. Complete mullerian agenesis (Choice B), also known as Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome, results from the failure of the mullerian duct to develop and presents with varying degrees of vaginal and uterine agenesis. Functioning ovaries are present and secondary sexual characteristics develop normally. A tender, midline mass would not be present in this disorder. Hormonally active ovarian tumor (Choice C) describes a category of sex-cord stromal tumors such as granulosa cell tumors, theca cell tumors, and Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors. These tumors may present with a palpable adnexal mass, abnormal uterine bleeding (especially in the case of the estrogen-producing granulosa cell tumor), or evidence of hyperandrogenism. This patient's clinical examination findings are more suggestive of an imperforate hymen with hematocolpos. Normal development (Choice E) is contradicted by the delayed onset of menarche in this patient. Menarche typically occurs between ages 11 and 14. Failure to develop menarche by age 16 is suggestive of primary amenorrhea. Educational Objective: lmperforate hymen is a congenital absence of the hymenal opening, which may present with primary amenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, and a bulging pelvic mass in an adolescent with otherwise normal sexual development. Surgical hymenotomy and evacuation of accumulated menstrual blood products is curative. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1, at 36 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital after she was found to have fetal growth restriction during a routine prenatal visit. She has a 6-year history of mild chronic essential hypertension controlled with 13-adrenergic blocking agents that were discontinued at 8 weeks' gestation . At 10 weeks' gestation , a 24-hour urine collection shows a protein concentration of 50 mg and creatinine clearance of 110 mUmin . Ultrasonography and amniocentesis at 18 weeks' gestation showed no abnormalities ; the estimated fetal weight was at the 50th percentile . Her temperature today is 36.6°C (97.8°F), pulse is 88/min , respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a fundal height of 30 cm. Ultrasonography shows a fetal head circumference consistent in size with a 35-week gestation and an abdominal circumference consistent in size with a 30-week gestation . The estimated fetal weight is at the 9th percentile . Which of the following is the most appropriate test to determine the risk of intrauterine fetal demise?

choices.D: Doppler ultrasonography of the umbilical arte~
choices.E: Determination of amniotic fluid glucose concentration

correctExplanation: Fetal growth restriction (FGR) occurs when the fetus fails to reach its full genetic growth potential due to a variety of maternal, fetal, or environmental factors. FGR is defined as an estimated fetal weight less than the 10th percentile and is classified as symmetrical or asymmetrical. In cases of symmetrical FGR, there is restriction of growth of the fetal head, abdomen, and extremities indicating continual impairment of fetal growth from an early stage of the gestation. Causes of symmetrical FGR include intrauterine infections, chromosomal abnormalities, and maternal drug or toxin exposures. In cases of asymmetrical FGR there is normal development of the fetal head with restricted growth of the fetal abdomen and extremities. Asymmetrical FGR typically occurs in the third trimester from causes such as maternal hypertension, chronic kidney disease, preeclampsia, or smoking. Asymmetric FGR is the more common pattern and is usually late onset, often as a consequence of placental insufficiency. Fetuses and newborns affected by FGR are at an increased risk of intrauterine fetal demise. This fetus displays evidence of asymmetric FGR, which is best evaluated by Doppler ultrasonography of the umbilical artery to assess for fetal well-being in the third trimester. Doppler ultrasonography can be used to evaluate the umbilical artery waveform to assess for placental insufficiency, and it has been shown to decrease perinatal morbidity and mortality.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Determination of nuchal thickness (Choice A) is performed by ultrasonography. An increased nuchal fold thickness may suggest the presence of a fetal chromosomal abnormality, but it is not useful in the evaluation of fetal growth restriction. Nuchal fold thickness is commonly increased in trisomy 21. A fetal fibronectin test (Choice B) is performed via vaginal swab and indicates leakage of fibronectin, a glycoprotein that is produced at the interface between the chorioamnion and the uterine decidua. Leakage of fetal fibronectin indicates an increased risk of impending preterm labor. A glucose tolerance test (Choice C) is useful for the diagnosis of maternal gestational diabetes. While gestational diabetes can lead to fetal growth restriction, it more commonly leads to fetal macrosomia. Evaluation for placental insufficiency with Doppler ultrasonography of the umbilical cord is therefore a more appropriate test than a glucose tolerance test. Determination of amniotic fluid glucose concentration (Choice E) is useful for identifying gestational diabetes or chorioamnionitis. It is not useful for the diagnosis of fetal growth restriction. Educational Objective: Fetal growth restriction occurs when the fetus fails to reach its genetically determined growth potential and is defined by an estimated fetal weight less than the 10th percentile. When occurring in the third trimester, it may indicate fetal hypoxia secondary to maternal vascular risk factors. Umbilical Doppler ultrasonography is the best test to evaluate for potential uteroplacental insufficiency as a cause. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 23-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of pain and burning with urination . Two years ago, she had similar symptoms that resolved with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole therapy. She is sexually active and uses an oral contraceptive . Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Examination shows no costovertebral angle tenderness . Urinalysis shows bacteria and pus. She requests advice about preventing future episodes . Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.A: Drinking 6 ounces of cranberry juice daily

correctExplanation: Lower urinary tract infections (UTls) present with dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort. They occur more frequently in women than in men because of a shorter urethra and favorable regional environment for bacterial growth. Risk factors include the presence of a urinary catheter, anatomic genitourinary defects, diabetes, pregnancy, and frequent or recent sexual intercourse. Urinalysis will typically show bacteriuria, white blood cells, positive leukocyte esterase, and positive nitrites depending on the infectious organism. Treatment of uncomplicated UTls typically consists of outpatient antibiotic management with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, nitrofurantoin, or cephalexin. Preventive measures for UTls include voiding immediately after coitus, oral hydration, and improvement of feminine hygiene practices to reduce the introduction of bacteria to the urethra.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Drinking 6 ounces of cranberry juice daily (Choice A) has not been shown to decrease the frequency of recurrent urinary tract infections. Antibiotic prophylaxis only after coitus (Choice C) or daily trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis (Choice D) are adequate regimens to prevent recurrent urinary tract infections. However, as this patient has only had two urinary tract infections in two years, voiding after coitus would be a better initial option for preventing recurrence without the risk of antibiotic adverse effects. No preventive measures available (Choice E) is not correct, as there are a number of behavioral and medical interventions that can be taken to reduce the risk of recurrent UTls. Educational Objective: Lower urinary tract infections (UTls) typically present with dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort, more frequently in women than in men. Prevention includes voiding immediately after coitus, oral hydration, and improvement in feminine hygiene practices to reduce the introduction of bacteria into the urethra. Prophylactic antibiotics are an option for recurrent UTls that do not respond to more conservative prevention techniques. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination . Six weeks ago, she underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for leiomyomata uteri. She has no history of abnormal Pap smears . Examination today shows a well-healing incision . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step regarding future Pap smears for this patient?

choices.B: Annually for 3 years and then every 3 years
choices.D: In 1 year and then no longer indicated

correctExplanation: Pap smear testing employs a cervical swab to collect cells from the transformation zone of the cervix and is an important screening tool for the detection of cervical carcinoma. The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) guidelines recommend screening for cervical carcinoma with Pap smear testing alone every 3 years in women between 21 and 29 years of age. Pap smear testing is also recommended every 3 years in women between 30 and 65 years of age or every 5 years if co-testing for human papillomavirus (HPV) is also performed. Total abdominal hysterectomy involves the surgical removal of the uterus and the cervix. Patients who have undergone this procedure for a benign indication such as uterine fibroids no longer require cervical cancer screening with Pap smears because they no longer have cervical tissue.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Annual screening (Choice A) or annually for 3 years and then every 3 years (Choice B) are intensified screening regimens that may be appropriate for certain high-risk patients, such as those with a history of previously resected or ablated cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, HIV, or maternal exposure to diethylstilbestrol. These intensified screening regimens are not required in a patient who has undergone total abdominal hysterectomy for a benign indication without an additional condition to merit ongoing screening. Screening every 3 years (Choice C) is recommended for women between the ages of 21 and 29. Screening every 3 years is also recommended for women between 30 and 65 years of age if co-testing for HPV is not performed. However, this is not appropriate after total abdominal hysterectomy for a benign indication as the patient no longer has cervical tissue. Screening in 1 year and then no longer (Choice D) is not appropriate after total abdominal hysterectomy for a benign indication as the patient no longer has cervical tissue. Educational Objective: Total abdominal hysterectomy involves surgical removal of the uterus and cervix. Patients who have undergone this procedure for a benign condition do not require further screening for cervical cancer. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 20-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1, at 42 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor. She reports severe abdominal pain. She has received no prenatal care. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . Leopold maneuvers indicate a fetus at term. The cervix is 10 cm dilated and 100% effaced ; the vertex is at +2 station . After pushing for 3 hours, low-forceps-assisted delivery is performed because of nonreassuring fetal heart tones , severe variable decelerations , and maternal exhaustion . The operative vaginal delivery of a 4200-g (9.3-lb) newborn is complicated by shoulder dystocia that requires 8 minutes to reduce. On examination , the newborn does not move the right arm. The forearm is pronated , and the arm is adducted and internally rotated at the shoulder. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings in this newborn?

choices.B: Hypoxic injury to the motor area of the precentral gyrus
choices.C: Injury to the eighth cervical root and first thoracic root
choices.D: Injury to the fifth and sixth cervical roots

correctExplanation: Erb palsy is characterized by a pronated, adducted, and internally rotated arm secondary to an injury of the upper brachia! plexus fifth and sixth cervical roots (C5, C6). This can occur during delivery as lateral traction is placed on the neck during a complicated birth, as in cases of shoulder dystocia or forceps-assisted delivery. The C5 and C6 roots control the deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and biceps brachii muscles. Loss of function of these muscles leads to adduction of the arm caused by failure of the deltoid and supraspinatus to abduct the arm, medial rotation of the arm caused by failure of the infraspinatus to externally rotate the arm, and extension and pronation of the arm caused by the failure of the biceps brachii to flex and supinate the forearm.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Fracture of the clavicle (Choice A) can be a complication of shoulder dystocia, or in extreme cases, it may be an intentional maneuver to help deliver a baby. Clavicle fractures can cause pain and decreased movement of the affected extremity, but they typically heal in 1 to 2 weeks. Hypoxic injury to the motor area of the precentral gyrus (Choice B) would present with paralysis of the contralateral face and extremities. The precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe contains pyramidal neurons that function as the primary motor cortex of the brain responsible for executing voluntary movements. Rather, this patient shows signs suspicious for a palsy of specific peripheral nerves. Injury to the eighth cervical root and first thoracic root (Choice C) is often referred to as Klumpke palsy and can occur during a delivery requiring an upward force on the newborn's arm. This injury leads to a dysfunction of the intrinsic hand muscles, including the lumbricals, interossei, and hypothenar muscles. Partial dislocation of the elbow (Choice E) can be subtle to detect, presenting with pain with movement of the elbow joint, not the characteristic palsy of muscles associated with roots C5 and C6. Educational Objective: Erb palsy is a brachia! plexus injury of the C5 and C6 nerve roots caused by lateral traction of the neck during delivery. This results in dysfunction of the deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and biceps brachii muscles, presenting as characteristic arm adduction, internal rotation, extension, and pronation. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 42-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus comes to the physician for a follow-up examination . Two weeks ago, prednisone therapy was begun because of a flare-up of her disease; this is her third course of prednisone during the past 18 months . Today, the patient is feeling well. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals . Her only other medications are vitamin D and calcium . She has no other history of serious illness , and there is no family history of serious illness. She has no known allergies . She does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 63 kg (140 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m 2. Her pulse is 70/min , and blood pressure is 108/64 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to prevent osteoporosis in this patient?

choices.D: Estrogen alone at the onset of menopause

correctExplanation: Glucocorticoids significantly alter calcium metabolism by decreasing gastrointestinal calcium absorption, enhancing osteoclastogenesis, and inhibiting osteoblast differentiation. Primary prevention of osteoporosis is indicated in patients with chronic glucocorticoid use to prevent premature, pathologic fragility fractures. Vitamin D and calcium are recommended for all patients at low risk of fracture. In addition to calcium and vitamin D, patients at moderate to high risk of fracture are also treated with oral bisphosphonates (eg, alendronate). Bisphosphonates have been shown to reduce fracture risk and increase bone density. They are the mainstay of osteoporosis treatment and prevention in patients that are at moderate to high risk for bone mineral density loss because of corticosteroid use. Bisphosphonates act to inhibit the action of osteoclasts, thereby preventing bone loss.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Calcitonin {Choice B) is a peptide hormone that decreases osteoclast activity and osteoclast differentiation, thereby reducing bone resorption. However, it is significantly less effective than bisphosphonates. It is therefore not a first-line treatment for osteoporosis or prevention of glucocorticoid-induced bone loss. Estrogen and progesterone now {Choice C) and estrogen therapy alone at the onset of menopause {Choice D) are no longer generally recommended for the prevention or treatment of osteoporosis; the Women's Health Initiative showed that hormone therapy increases the risk of thromboembolic events in postmenopausal women. In low risk cases, estrogen therapy may still be used for a short duration and at a low dose for the treatment of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women less than 60 years of age who have a low risk of stroke or blood clot and who wish to treat the symptoms of menopause. Raloxifene {Choice E) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator that acts as an estrogen agonist in bone and as an antagonist in breast and endometrial tissue. It may be used for the prevention of osteoporosis in women at high risk for breast cancer, however, it carries an increased risk for venous thromboembolic events. Therefore, it is not ideal in a patient predisposed to thrombosis due to a known inflammatory state (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus) and at risk of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome. Educational Objective: Bisphosphonates, along with calcium and vitamin D, decrease the risk of osteoporosis and reduce bone mineral density loss in osteoporotic patients. Prolonged glucocorticoid use is a key risk factor in the development of osteoporosis due to decreased gastrointestinal calcium absorption, increased osteoclastogenesis, and diminished differentiation of osteoblasts. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 4 7-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician because of heavy menstrual flow during the past 3 months. Previous menses were normal with regard to flow. She has mild hypertension treated with diuretics and type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with oral hypoglycemics . She has no history of abnormal Pap smears . She is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 95 kg (210 lb); BMI is 37 kg/m 2• Her blood pressure is 146/86 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities . A Pap smear is reported as atypical glandular cells. Colposcopy shows no abnormalities . Endocervical curettage shows benign cells. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.E: Loop electrosurgical excision of the cervical transformation zone

correctExplanation: Abnormal uterine bleeding should be suspected when bleeding is irregular, unpredictable, or not associated with usual menstrual signs and symptoms (eg, bloating, breast fullness, uterine cramps). It may be caused by structural abnormalities such as cervical or endometrial polyps, adenomyosis, endometrial hyperplasia, malignancy, inflammation or infection of the genital tract, coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, or endocrine dysfunction (eg, thyroid disorders, prolactin, androgens). It may also be iatrogenic or idiopathic. The patient has no symptoms or history of thyroid disorder, coagulopathy, polycystic ovary syndrome, or other ovulatory dysfunction. In patients over 45 years of age, there is a higher risk for endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy. The patient has atypical glandular cells on Pap smear and has been evaluated for cervical malignancy with colposcopy and endocervical curettage, which showed no abnormalities. The next appropriate step in evaluation would be an endometrial biopsy to evaluate the risk of endometrial cancer. If a patient cannot tolerate an outpatient procedure or if the outpatient sampling is nondiagnostic, a dilation and curettage or hysteroscopy can be performed. A hysteroscopy with sampling allows for a more complete evaluation of the endometrium (eg, polyps, myomas, structural abnormalities).
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Second Pap smear in 6 months (Choice A) would not be the appropriate next step because the Pap smear already shows atypical glandular cells. Repeat Pap smear and cytology would be the next step in management for women with atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US). For women with ASC-US, another option would be human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing (Choice B). If HPV is detected, colposcopy is the next appropriate step. If HPV is not detected, a repeat Pap smear is done in 12 months. Pelvic ultrasonography (Choice C) can be helpful in evaluating endometrial hyperplasia, polyps, myomas, and other structural abnormalities of the uterus. An endometrial thickness of greater than 4 mm in a postmenopausal patient, a polypoid mass, or fluid collection is indication for further evaluation and sampling. Given the presence of glandular cells on sampling, the best next step would be a biopsy to evaluate the cause of the atypical cells. Loop electrosurgical excision of the cervical transformation zone (Choice E) would be done if colposcopy or endocervical curettage showed a cervical cause of the atypical Pap smear findings. Educational Objective: Abnormal uterine bleeding may be caused by structural, neoplastic, coagulopathic, infectious, endocrine, or iatrogenic sources. After an abnormal Pap smear showing atypical glandular cells, the next appropriate steps in evaluation includes colposcopy and endocervical curettage. If these are normal, an endometrial biopsy is necessary to evaluate for endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 1, with recently diagnosed breast cancer comes to the physician for advice regarding contraception . She will begin chemotherapy and radiation therapy in 6 weeks . She had been using a combination oral contraceptive for 3 years but discontinued it 8 weeks ago on advice of her oncologist and began using condoms . Since discontinuing oral contraceptive therapy, she has had one menstrual period that lasted 4 days. Previously , menses occurred at regular 28-day intervals and lasted 3 to 4 days. She delivered her first child 18 months ago and wishes to have another child in the future . She has no other history of serious illness and takes no other medications . Her blood pressure is 115/72 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding contraception for this patient?
correctExplanation: Placement of a copper IUD is a long-acting reversible contraceptive option that can be used in patients with breast malignancy. Breast cancers may express estrogen, progesterone, or HER2 receptor positivity. Depending on the receptor positivity of the patient's breast malignancy, hormonal contraceptives may be harmful and increase the risk for breast cancer progression. The copper IUD provides a contraceptive method without the use of hormones. Copper is spermicidal and inhibits sperm motility and the acrosomal reaction necessary for fertilization. As well, it induces local inflammatory changes of the endometrium and increases cervical mucus production, further decreasing the chance of successful sperm passage or embryonic implantation in the endometrium. The IUD can be kept in place for up to ten years and the rate of pregnancy is less than 1 %. Potential complications include increased menstrual flow and pain during menses. Contraindications to copper IUD insertion include copper allergy, Wilson disease, endometrial cancer, and undiagnosed abnormal uterine bleeding.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hormonal contraceptives include combination ethinyl estradiol and progestin oral contraceptives, progestin-only oral contraceptives (Choice A), and depot medroxyprogesterone (Choice D), which is an injectable progestin that lasts for 14 weeks and results in a sustained release of progestin to prevent pregnancy. Etonogestrel implant (Choice E) is another long-acting hormonal contraceptive that is placed subcutaneously in the upper arm. Hormonal contraceptives are contraindicated in thromboembolic disorders, liver dysfunction, and breast malignancy with estrogen or progesterone receptor positivity. A diaphragm (Choice B) is a barrier contraceptive that fits on top of the cervix and anterior wall of the vagina. It must be placed prior to intercourse and left in for 6 to 8 hours after use. It is typically used with spermicide. A diaphragm is not as effective at preventing pregnancy compared to an IUD. It also carries an increased risk of urinary tract infection due to pressure on the urethra and use of the spermicide, which would be unsuitable in a patient undergoing immunosuppressive therapy with chemotherapy and radiation. Educational Objective: Hormonal contraceptives are contraindicated in breast malignancy with estrogen or progesterone receptor positivity. A copper IUD is effective and does not contain hormones. It is spermicidal, inhibiting sperm motility and the acrosomal reaction necessary for fertilization. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: At 37 weeks' gestation , a 28-year-old woman with gestational diabetes delivers a 4500-g (10-lb) newborn who develops hyaline membrane disease . The mother had postprandial serum glucose concentrations of 180-200 mg/dl during the last half of pregnancy . The macrosomia and pulmonary disease are most closely related to an increased serum concentration of which of the following in the fetus?
correctExplanation: Excessive fetal exposure to insulin in utero can cause macrosomia and hyaline membrane disease, also called neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Human placental lactogen produced by the placenta increases maternal insulin resistance. Gestational diabetes occurs when the mother's body cannot generate enough insulin to overcome the insulin resistance. This leads to an increased concentration of glucose in the maternal circulation, and subsequently the fetal circulation. Fetal hyperglycemia in turn causes the fetus to produce excess insulin. The insulin then acts as a growth factor, leading to macrosomia. The insulin also inhibits the production of surfactant, and this relative deficiency leads to increased alveolar surface tension, alveolar collapse, and hyaline membrane disease marked by fetal respiratory distress, hypoxia, rhonchi on auscultation, and diffuse alveolar infiltrates on imaging. Risk factors for gestational diabetes include obesity, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), previous gestational diabetes, and African American, Asian American, Hispanic, Native American, and Pacific Islander ethnicity.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cortisol {Choice A) is a hormone synthesized in the adrenal cortex. It has a multitude of effects, including increasing blood pressure, insulin resistance, and gluconeogenesis, and decreasing inflammation and the immune response. Excess concentrations are seen in Cushing syndrome which presents with weight gain, hypertension, hirsutism, striae, osteoporosis, and hyperglycemia. It does not cause macrosomia or hyaline membrane disease. Growth hormone {Choice B) is known to increase insulin resistance in addition to its primary function of increasing bone growth and muscle mass via insulin-like growth factor-1 {IGF-1). Excess growth hormone leads to gigantism in children and acromegaly in adults but requires a prolonged period of exposure to exert its effect and thus, would not be evident immediately at birth. Human placental lactogen {Choice C) is a hormone produced by the placenta that increases maternal insulin resistance. It continues to rise throughout pregnancy, peaking just before birth. It plays a role in the development of gestational diabetes, but it does not directly cause macrosomia or hyaline membrane disease. Reverse triiodothyronine (rT :il {Choice E) is the inactive isomer of triiodothyronine, which exhibits no physiologic activity. The concentration of rT 3 increases in euthyroid sick syndrome. It is not associated with gestational diabetes. Educational Objective: Gestational diabetes occurs in the second half of pregnancy, with risk factors including obesity, PCOS, previous gestational diabetes, and genetic or ethnic predisposition. Complications include macrosomia and hyaline membrane disease secondary to an increase in fetal insulin exposure, as well as preterm birth, hypoglycemia in the newborn, and fetal mortality. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 26-year-old nulligravid woman has had infertility for 2 years . Menses occur at regular 25-day intervals . Serum progesterone concentration is 8 ng/ml (N>5) on menstrual day 21 . An endometrial biopsy specimen on menstrual day 24 is most likely to show which of the following in this patient?
correctExplanation: Secretory endometrium occurs during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle, or the 14 days prior to menstruation. The first half of the menstrual cycle, the follicular phase, which varies in length, begins with menses. During menses, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) concentrations increase and stimulate the developing follicle. The follicle produces estrogen, which leads to proliferation of the endometrium in preparation for implantation of a fertilized ovum. As estrogen rises, a surge occurs, which in turn stimulates a surge in LH that causes ovulation. Immediately following ovulation, the luteal phase begins as the corpus luteum forms. The corpus luteum secretes progesterone to maintain the endometrial lining. If no implantation occurs, the corpus luteum degrades to the corpus albicans and estrogen and progesterone concentrations decrease, causing menstruation and minor increases in FSH and LH. Since this patient's progesterone is within the reference range and the biopsy is occurring four days before her regularly expected menstrual period, the biopsy would most likely show secretory endometrium.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Atrophic endometrium (Choice A) refers to a decrease in the normal amount of endometrial tissue, commonly seen in postmenopausal women because of a decrease in estrogen. This patient is still having regular periods, making atrophic endometrium unlikely on biopsy. Decidual endometrium (Choice B) forms from the endometrium following implantation of an embryo. It is stimulated by progesterone and forms the maternal part of the placenta. As this patient is not pregnant, a biopsy would not show decidual endometrium. Hyperplasia of endometrium (Choice C) is an increase in endometrial growth, commonly caused by an excessive amount of estrogen. Symptoms include heavy vaginal bleeding or postmenopausal bleeding. Risk factors include late menopause, nulliparity, early menarche, obesity, and the exogenous use of estrogen. Proliferative endometrium (Choice D) occurs during the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle in response to estrogen causing a gradual growth in the endometrial lining. However, as this patient is nearing her menses, a biopsy would more likely show secretory rather than proliferative endometrium. Educational Objective: The endometrium proceeds through three stages during each menstrual cycle: menses, proliferative, and secretory. Proliferative endometrium occurs immediately after menses during the follicular phase because of increased estrogen concentration. However, following ovulation 14 days prior to menstruation, the endometrium transitions to the secretory stage during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 4 7-year-old woman has had increasing fatigue , constipation , night sweats , anxiety, and mood !ability over the past year; she has had a 2.3-kg (5-lb) weight gain during this period . Her last menstrual period was 6 months ago. Her blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Physical and pelvic examinations show normal findings . Which of the following serum concentrations is most likely to be increased?
correctExplanation: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) begins to increase with the start of menopause. While menopause is defined by the absence of menstruation for 12 months, symptoms can begin prior to menstrual cessation. It primarily presents in women aged 40 to 50, but premature menopause can occur in women less than 40 years of age, especially in those who smoke. Common symptoms include hot flashes, night sweats, irritability, mood changes, vaginal atrophy, and loss of libido. Menopause occurs secondary to exhaustion of ovarian follicles, with subsequent anovulation and decreased estrogen concentration. In response, FSH and luteinizing hormone (LH) lack negative feedback and are increased in the serum as a result. Menopause is often a clinical diagnosis, but these laboratory values may be obtained if the diagnosis is unclear. Hormone therapy or selective serotonin/norepinephrine inhibitors (SSRls/SNRls) can be used to treat the vasomotor symptoms of menopause, but hormone therapy has been attributed to an increased risk of breast cancer, hypercoagulability, and cardiovascular mortality.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. ACTH (Choice A), or adrenocorticotropic hormone, is increased in some subtypes of Cushing syndrome, which subsequently increases cortisol concentration. Typical features of Cushing syndrome include weight gain, oligomenorrhea, central obesity, skin striae, moon facies, and increased truncal fat deposition. Hypertension and insulin resistance can also occur. While this patient does have weight gain, her symptoms do not otherwise fit a diagnosis of Cushing syndrome. Parathyroid hormone (Choice C) is increased in hyperparathyroidism, which presents with differing effects on calcium and phosphate concentrations depending on whether the patient has primary, secondary, or tertiary disease. Primary hyperparathyroidism presents with abdominal and bone pain, psychological changes, and nephrolithiasis. Secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism are most commonly related to chronic kidney disease. Parathyroid hormone is unlikely to be increased in this patient. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (Choice D) and thyrotropin-releasing hormone (Choice E) are increased in primary hypothyroidism, which most frequently presents with fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, and oligomenorrhea. Physical examination may disclose bradycardia, dry, edematous skin, and delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes. It does not cause night sweats, and menopause would be more likely in a woman in her late forties presenting with night sweats and amenorrhea. Educational Objective: Menopause commonly presents in women aged 40 to 50 with amenorrhea, night sweats, irritability or mood !ability, and weight gain due to the exhaustion of ovarian follicle reserves and decreased estrogen concentration. While it commonly is a clinical diagnosis, increased serum FSH and LH concentrations can be useful in establishing the diagnosis. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 28-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 1, has been amenorrheic and has had hot flashes for the past 6 months. She takes thyroid medication for chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis (Hashimoto disease) . After using an oral contraceptive for 2 years , she discontinued taking it 3 years ago. Serum studies show: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
correctExplanation: Follicle-stimulating hormone Estradiol Thyroid-stimulating hormone Prolactin 62 mlU/mL 15 pg/ml (N=20-60) 1.5 µU/ml 5 ng/ml Autoimmune ovarian failure, also known as primary ovarian insufficiency, classically presents in a woman of reproductive age with anovulation, amenorrhea, and infertility. It can also present with signs of early menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, and irregular bleeding. It is caused by autoimmune inflammation and destruction within the ovaries, leading to a decrease in estrogen production, diminished follicle reserve, and loss of ovarian stromal cells. Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) are appropriately increased because of the lack of negative feedback from estrogen on the anterior pituitary, as is seen in this case. It is most often idiopathic but is more common in women with karyotype abnormalities or other autoimmune diseases such as chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hypothalamic dysfunction (Choice B) can also lead to anovulation and amenorrhea by virtue of decreased gonadotropin-releasing hormone, which subsequently leads to decreased FSH and LH concentrations. It is a common cause of amenorrhea or anovulation in young athletes. Inadequate control of hypothyroidism (Choice C) can also cause amenorrhea and infertility. However, the patient's TSH concentration is within normal limits. This indicates that her thyroid supplementation is adequate. Post-pill amenorrhea (Choice D) is a common period of anovulation and amenorrhea following discontinuation of long-term oral contraceptive medications. Combined oral contraceptives contain estrogen and progesterone, and their steady effects on the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis prevent ovulation or implantation of a fertilized oocyte, thereby preventing pregnancy. After discontinuing oral contraceptives, it may take several months for the normal hormone cycle to resume. However, this patient discontinued oral contraceptives three years ago, making persistent post-pill amenorrhea unlikely. Pure gonadal dysgenesis (Choice E) is defined by the absence of functional ovarian tissue (eg, atrophic gonads). It presents with amenorrhea and absence of secondary sexual characteristics, and results of laboratory studies will show decreased estrogen concentration and increased FSH and LH concentrations. As this patient previously was able to conceive, she does not have pure gonadal dysgenesis. Educational Objective: Autoimmune ovarian failure or primary ovarian insufficiency presents in reproductive-age women with anovulation, amenorrhea, and infertility. Results of laboratory studies show decreased estrogen and increased FSH and LH concentration. It is commonly associated with other autoimmune disorders or karyotype abnormalities. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A sexually active 21-year-old college student requests an oral contraceptive . There are no contraindications based on her medical history. In addition to a Pap smear, which of the following screening tests is most appropriate?

choices.C: Measurement of fasting serum glucose concentration

correctExplanation: Testing for Chlamydia trachomatis, as well as for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, is recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) for all sexually active patients under 25 years old. C. Trachomatis is a sexually transmitted infection that classically presents with urethritis, dysuria, and urethral or vaginal discharge. However, it can also be asymptomatic. Complications include cervicitis, epididymitis, reactive arthritis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. Gram stain of the urine or urethral/vaginal discharge typically does not reveal organisms, as C. trachomatis is an obligate intracellular organism. Diagnosis is made with a nucleic acid amplification test, and treatment consists of either azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone, with the latter covering a potential N. gonorrhoeae coinfection .
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Liver function tests (Choice B) would not be indicated in this patient. The patient has no risk factors for or symptoms related to liver dysfunction. A baseline level is not necessary prior to initiating oral contraceptives, as liver toxicity is an exceedingly rare adverse effect of oral contraceptive therapy. Measurement of fasting serum glucose concentration (Choice C) is used to diagnose diabetes mellitus. Common symptoms include increased thirst, frequent urination, weight loss, fatigue, and frequent infections. The patient does not have signs or symptoms of diabetes and measuring serum glucose concentration is not warranted based on USPSTF guidelines for her demographic. Assay for serum HIV antibodies (Choice D) to screen for HIV infection may eventually be appropriate, as the USPSTF and the Center for Disease Control recommend that everyone between the teenage years and age 65 be tested at least once. Those at higher risk (men who have sex with men, or those with multiple sexual partners, having sex in exchange for money or drugs, or using condoms inconsistently) should be screened more frequently. This patient would benefit more from testing for C. trachomatis at this time, as it is a more common infection and more frequently presents asymptomatically, though HIV testing should also eventually be performed. The serologic test for syphilis (Choice E) is not recommended in asymptomatic patients. Syphilis has a multitude of presentations depending on its stage. Primary syphilis can present with a genital lesion that is nonpainful, while secondary syphilis presents with a maculopapular rash and condyloma lata. Tertiary syphilis, the most advanced form, has symptoms of neurosyphilis (eg, tabes dorsalis, Argyll Robertson pupil, ataxia) and aortitis. The patient is not experiencing any of these symptoms. Educational Objective: Annual screening for C. trachomatis is recommended in all sexually active patients under 25 years of age. It typically presents with urethral or vaginal discharge, dysuria, and dyspareunia if it has progressed to cervicitis . Complications also include epididymitis, reactive arthritis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. It is treated with azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone, with the latter covering a potential N. gonorrhoeae coinfection. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 2, at 30 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department because of pain in the right mid abdomen for 12 hours; she has had one episode of diarrhea since that time . Her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F). Physical examination shows diffuse tenderness in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen with minimal guarding . Rectal and pelvic examinations show right-sided tenderness . Her leukocyte count is 14,000/mm 3 with a shift to the left. Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows fluid in the right paracolic gutter; the appendix cannot be visualized . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Appendicitis typically presents with right lower quadrant abdominal pain that is often periumbilical at onset, with associated nausea, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis, and tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant on examination. In pregnancy, due to the location of the enlarging uterus, the appendix may be displaced superiorly as compared to that of a nongravid patient. This displacement limits the classic history and physical examination, which rely on a right lower quadrant position of the appendix. For example, initial periumbilical pain is attributed to vague, visceral innervation of the appendix being referred to the midline; once inflammation affects the parietal peritoneum, the pain becomes well-localized to the right lower quadrant, hence, the migratory character. McBurney point, a sensitive location for tenderness on palpation, is located at one-third the distance between the inguinal ligament and the umbilicus because this is the common position of the appendix. When displaced cephalad, the parietal peritoneal inflammation may no longer occur at the McBurney point, even migrating as far as the right upper quadrant, mimicking diagnoses such as cholecystitis. Diagnosis is facilitated by CT scan (though less ideal in pregnancy due to the risk of teratogenicity to the fetus), MRI, or ultrasonography, which may show appendiceal enlargement, the presence of an appendicolith, appendiceal wall thickening, or periappendiceal fluid. Fluid in the paracolic gutter is suggestive of appendiceal rupture or perforation and is typically accompanied by rising fever and leukocytosis. Immediate surgical exploration and appendectomy is indicated to prevent significant maternal and fetal complications including peritonitis, sepsis, and death.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cultures of the stool (Choice A) are appropriate for the diagnosis of infectious enterocolitis, which may present with abdominal pain, fever, and leukocytosis. However, infectious enterocolitis would generally not present with focal right lower quadrant abdominal pain, or fluid in the paracolic gutter. Barium enema (Choice B) and sigmoidoscopy (Choice D) may be useful in the diagnosis of diverticulosis, colorectal cancer, or inflammatory bowel disease. Delaying surgical exploration in order to pursue further imaging studies is not appropriate given the patient's clinical presentation, which is suggestive of appendicitis with appendiceal rupture. Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy and observation (Choice C) are appropriate treatment options for uncomplicated appendicitis in select patients. This strategy is not appropriate in gravid patients and is associated with a lower success rate compared to surgical appendectomy, which remains the standard of care. Surgical exploration is mandatory once appendiceal perforation is suspected or has occurred. Educational Objective: Acute appendicitis may occur in gravid women and presents with variably located right-sided pain based on the location of the appendix or periumbilical abdominal pain. It is also associated with nausea, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis, and tenderness to palpation. Fluid in the paracolic gutter on ultrasonography is suggestive of appendiceal rupture, which is managed with emergency surgical exploration. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal cramps . Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She is sexually active with one partner, and they use condoms for contraception consistently . She takes no medications . Her pulse is 90/min , and blood pressure is 100/65 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a soft abdomen and lower quadrant tenderness . Speculum examination shows moderate vaginal bleeding and a closed cervical os. A pregnancy test is positive . Transvaginal ultrasonography shows a fluid-filled endometrial cavity and no gestational sac. Her quantitative serum 13-hCG concentration is 2500 mlU/mL. Forty-eight hours later, a second measurement of quantitative serum 13-hCG concentration is 2800 mlU/mL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Pregnancy is suspected when there is a missed or delayed menstrual period, and ectopic pregnancy often presents with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain. Serum 13-hCG is produced by the placenta, is undetectable in nonpregnant patients, and doubles approximately every 48 hours during an early normal pregnancy. Ectopic pregnancy is an abnormal pregnancy in which the fertilized ovum implants in the fallopian tube (most common), on the ovary, within the peritoneal cavity, or in any non-endometrial location. 13-hCG concentration does not increase as expected in ectopic pregnancy, often lagging the normal expected doubling. Ultrasonography can be used to assess for an intrauterine pregnancy and may show an ectopic pregnancy; in a normal pregnancy, an intrauterine gestational sac should be visible by 5 weeks' gestation. Additionally, transvaginal ultrasonography provides sufficient sensitivity to detect an intrauterine pregnancy once the 13-hCG concentration exceeds 1000 to 2000 mlU/mL. An ectopic pregnancy is not viable. Treatment of an ectopic pregnancy can be medical with methotrexate for small, early pregnancies, but may require salpingectomy or evacuation with laparoscopy for larger pregnancies or in cases of medical treatment failure. Complications of ectopic pregnancy include rupture, bleeding, and hemoperitoneum.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Blighted ovum (Choice A) is an anembryonic pregnancy in which a fertilized egg attaches to the uterine wall and a gestational sac without an embryo develops. It may present with vaginal bleeding or may be asymptomatic, and serum 13-hCG concentration decreases with time. A complete spontaneous abortion (Choice B) would also present with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding with a delayed menstrual period. However, serum 13-hCG concentration should decrease, not increase, with a spontaneous abortion. Hydatidiform mole (Choice D) is a form of gestational trophoblastic disease characterized by non-invasive diffuse swelling of chorionic villi and the absence of fetal parts in the case of a complete mole. Complete moles contain purely paternal DNA. On ultrasonography, there may be an enlarged uterus with cystic structures without any specific fetal structures. Hydatidiform moles produce 13-hCG often in excess of proportion to gestational dates, which can be used as a biomarker. A normal intrauterine pregnancy (Choice E) may also present with abdominal pain and light vaginal bleeding or spotting in the first trimester due to implantation or threatened abortion. In a normal intrauterine pregnancy, serum 13-hCG concentration should double in 48 hours. Educational Objective: Ectopic pregnancy is an abnormal extrauterine pregnancy occurring in an anatomic location that cannot support the fetus (eg, in the fallopian tube, cervix, ovary, or peritoneum). It commonly presents with vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain, and an abnormally low serum 13-hCG, which in a normal pregnancy should double every 48 hours. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because she has never had a menstrual period . She is otherwise healthy. Both of her older sisters had normal pubertal development. Examination shows absent breast development and scant pubic hair. Her serum follicle -stimulating hormone concentration is 105 mlU/mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.D: Measurement of serum luteinizing hormone concentration
choices.E: Measurement of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration

correctExplanation: Turner syndrome is a common cause of primary amenorrhea, which is caused by ovarian dysgenesis in a 45, XO genotype. Other signs of Turner syndrome include a short stature, cystic hygroma or webbed neck, swelling in the hands or feet, coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, horseshoe kidney, and infertility. Additionally, due to decreased estrogen concentration, patients fail to develop secondary sexual characteristics. Vital signs will be within normal limits, and diagnosis is made through a karyotype analysis. Increased concentrations of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) due to the lack of negative feedback from estrogen may also aid in diagnosis, but these findings are nonspecific.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) stimulation test (Choice A) can be used to diagnose central precocious puberty(< 8 years in girls and < 9 years in boys) or, occasionally, delayed puberty. After giving a GnRH analog to patients, LH and FSH concentrations are measured. Turner syndrome is a form of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, and a GnRH-releasing stimulation test would not play a role in diagnosis. Measurement of serum electrolyte concentrations (Choice C) would not assist in the diagnosis of Turner syndrome as it is not characterized by serum electrolyte abnormalities. Measurement of serum luteinizing hormone concentration (Choice D) would be helpful in determining whether the patient's primary amenorrhea was hypergonadotropic or hypogonadotropic. However, it would not aid in the diagnosis of this patient, as the increased concentration of FSH already suggests hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. Measurement of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration (Choice E) would aid in the diagnosis of thyroid disorders. While both hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism can present with irregular menses, they are uncommon causes of primary amenorrhea. Educational Objective: Turner Syndrome (45, XO) is a common cause of primary amenorrhea, which is caused by ovarian dysgenesis. Other signs include the absence of secondary sexual characteristics, short stature, cystic hygroma or webbed neck, swelling in the hands or feet, coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, horseshoe kidney, and infertility. LH and FSH concentrations are increased because of the absence of negative feedback from estrogen, and diagnosis is made using a karyotype analysis. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 19-year-old primigravid woman comes to the emergency department because of a 1-week history of nausea and persistent vomiting . Her last menstrual period was 15 weeks ago , but she has had daily vaginal bleeding for the past month . She has not received prenatal care. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min , respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Examination shows pedal edema . Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 20-week gestation ; there is no adnexal tenderness . A serum pregnancy test is positive . Urinalysis shows 1 + protein . Ultrasonography shows bilateral multilocular ovarian cysts and echogenic structures in the uterus . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Hydatidiform moles are either caused by the fertilization of an empty egg by a single sperm followed by duplication of the paternal DNA resulting in 46 chromosomes (complete) or the dual fertilization of a normal ovum resulting in 69 chromosomes (incomplete). Maternal symptoms include hyperemesis gravidarum or persistent nausea and vomiting related to an abnormally increased 13-human chorionic gonadotropin (13- hCG) concentration. They can also cause first trimester vaginal bleeding, early preeclampsia, and uterine size greater than expected for dates. Complete moles contain no fetal tissue, while incomplete contain some fetal tissue. However, neither are viable pregnancies and no fetal heartbeat will be found on Doppler ultrasonography. Pelvic examination may show cystic molar clusters in the vagina, and laboratory studies will show an abnormally increased 13-hCG concentration. Ultrasonography of the pelvis will also show bilateral multilocular ovarian cysts (theca-lutein cysts) and echogenic structures in the uterus (hydatidiform molesy), as seen in this patient. Hydatidiform moles are treated with dilation and curettage, followed by appropriate contraception and sequential measurement of 13-hCG to monitor for the development of malignant gestational trophoblastic diseases such as invasive moles or choriocarcinoma. These malignant diseases are treated with chemotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Combined ectopic and intrauterine pregnancy (Choice A), also known as a heterotopic pregnancy, is extremely rare. It would likely present with abdominal pain and potential vaginal bleeding related to the ectopic extrauterine pregnancy. Ectopic pregnancies most commonly present early in pregnancy because of a restricted area for fetal development. An ultrasonography in this situation would show a viable intrauterine pregnancy in addition to an extrauterine ectopic pregnancy, most commonly in the fallopian tube. Multiple gestations (Choice C) can also present with hyperemesis gravidarum due to the increased maternal serum 13-hCG concentration. However, ultrasonography would show more than one viable fetus in the uterus. Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (Choice D) is an exaggerated follicular response to injected gonadotropins commonly used in infertility treatment. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and fluid retention, as well as shortness of breath and blood clots in severe cases. As this patient has not received injectable gonadotropins, this diagnosis is unlikely. Placenta accreta (Choice E) refers to the abnormal attachment of the placenta to the myometrium, rather than just the endometrium. Risk factors include prior cesarean delivery or uterine surgery, increased maternal age, and multiparity. Complications include postpartum hemorrhage due to the increased risk for retained products of conception. Polyhydramnios (Choice F) is an excessive amount of amniotic fluid. It is associated with maternal diabetes, multiple gestations, and fetal malformations such as esophageal or duodenal atresia and anencephaly. However, it is most commonly asymptomatic and would be associated with a viable uterine pregnancy, which is not seen in this patient. Educational Objective: Hydatidiform moles commonly present with persistent nausea and vomiting, first trimester vaginal bleeding, early preeclampsia, and uterine size out of proportion to the expected gestational age. Pelvic examination may show cystic clusters in the vagina. 13-hCG concentration will be markedly increased, and ultrasonography will show diffuse echogenic structures in the uterus and ovarian theca-lutein cysts. A hydatidiform mole can progress to malignant trophoblastic disease in the form of invasive moles or choriocarcinoma. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of irregular menses during the past 7 months. She also has had intense mood changes and occasional hot flashes during this time . Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago. She is sexually active with one male partner, and they usually use barrier contraception . Examination , including pelvic examination , shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Pregnancy should be considered as a cause of irregular menses in all women of reproductive age, especially in patients with irregular use of contraceptives. Pregnancy may be accompanied by symptoms including mood changes and hot flashes. In women with advanced maternal age, pregnancy must be excluded as a potential cause by obtaining a pregnancy test before proceeding with further evaluation of other causes such as menopause.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Measurement of serum estradiol (Choice A) and testosterone concentrations (Choice B) may detect hormonal changes associated with pregnancy or with disorders such as polycystic ovary syndrome, pituitary adenoma, or sex cord stromal tumors. A pregnancy test should be conducted before these conditions are considered. Transvaginal ultrasonography (Choice D) is useful for the evaluation of some causes of irregular menstruation, such as polycystic ovary syndrome or ovarian tumors. While transvaginal ultrasonography may identify an intrauterine pregnancy, a pregnancy test is a more sensitive initial test. Endometrial biopsy (Choice E) is useful for the evaluation of endometrial malignancy. In women of reproductive age, pregnancy must be excluded as a cause of irregular menstruation before considering more invasive diagnostic measures. Educational Objective: Pregnancy must be considered as a potential cause of irregular menstruation in all women of reproductive age. A pregnancy test is an inexpensive, rapid, and sensitive test for diagnosing pregnancy and should be obtained before proceeding with further workup. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 24-year-old primigravid woman at 42 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital for labor induction . Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated . She has no history of serious illness . On admission , her temperature is 36.9°C (98.5°F), pulse is 64/min , and blood pressure is 130/72 mm Hg. Fetal nonstress testing is reactive . Pelvic examination shows a closed , long, posterior cervix . The amniotic fluid index is 3.2 cm (N=9-31 ). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Discharge home and readmit in 1 week

correctExplanation: A pregnancy is considered postterm once a gestation extends to or beyond 42 weeks. Postterm pregnancy is associated with increased rates of maternal and neonatal complications, including meconium aspiration and fetal demise. While expectant management may be offered to select patients, the presence of an unfavorable cervix or oligohydramnios, as suggested by a low amniotic fluid index, are indications for induction of labor. Oligohydramnios may result from changes in maternal fetal circulation that occur because of the aging of the placenta. This is a known complication of postterm pregnancy and is associated with complications like umbilical cord compression. Induction of labor can be achieved by administering a prostaglandin analogue (eg. dinoprostone or misoprostol) or oxytocin. Nonpharmacologic methods of induction include stripping of the membranes and rupture of the amniotic sac.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Discharging the patient home and readmitting in 1 week (Choice A) is inappropriate given the presence of oligohydramnios in a postterm pregnancy. While uncomplicated postterm pregnancies may be managed expectantly, the presence of complications such as oligohydramnios is an indication for the induction of labor to reduce the risk of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. Administration of betamethasone (Choice B), a corticosteroid that stimulates fetal lung maturation and promotes fetal lung production of surfactant, is appropriate in preterm pregnancies. It has no role in the management of complicated postterm pregnancy. Amnioinfusion (Choice D) is the process of instilling fluid into the amniotic cavity. Amnioinfusion may be useful for the management of oligohydramnios, especially when fetal heart rate monitoring reveals variable decelerations suggestive of umbilical cord compression. In this case, amnioinfusion does not address the underlying cause of oligohydramnios, which is postterm pregnancy and maternal fetal circulatory changes caused by aging of the placenta. Induction of labor is therefore a more appropriate next step in management. Immediate cesarean delivery (Choice E) exposes the mother and fetus to unnecessary risks associated with surgery. Induction of labor is a more appropriate initial step. Immediate cesarean delivery is indicated if the induction of labor leads to fetal distress. Educational Objective: Postterm pregnancy is defined as a gestation that persists to or beyond 42 weeks and is associated with maternal and fetal complications. The presence of an unfavorable cervix or of complications such as oligohydramnios are indications for the induction of labor, which is achieved with a prostaglandin analogue (eg, dinoprostone or misoprostol) or with oxytocin. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: An 18-year-old woman comes to the physician because of irregular menses over the past 3 months ; menses occur at 14- to 40-day intervals . Menstrual flow varies from spotting to heavy cramping and bleeding; the latter symptoms have caused her to miss school. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. Menarche was at the age of 12 years , and menses had occurred at regular 28-day intervals for 6 years . She has a sedentary lifestyle . She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 63 kg (139 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m 2• Pelvic examination shows no abnormalities . A urine pregnancy test is negative . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Cyclic progesterone therapy is a key treatment in the management of anovulation. Common causes of anovulation include pregnancy, polycystic ovary syndrome, abnormalities or immaturity of the hypothalamic­ pituitary-ovarian axis, menopause or premature ovarian failure, inadequate nutrition, chromosomal abnormalities, and thyroid disorders. Anovulation presents with irregular intervals of menstruation associated with heavy vaginal bleeding when menses occur because of continued endometrial development. Progesterone therapy acts to inhibit follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH), preventing ovulation. Progesterone therapy also maintains the endometrial lining and causes its transition to a secretory, rather than proliferative, endometrium. When progesterone is withdrawn, bleeding occurs if the anovulation is caused by an abnormality or irregularity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, as is often the case in young women. Bleeding will not occur if the anovulation is caused by a structural abnormality of the uterus or estrogen deficiency.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Conjugated estrogen therapy (Choice A) is typically used to treat the vasomotor symptoms associated with menopause. Conjugated estrogen therapy is associated with an increased risk of breast cancer, hypercoagulability, and cardiovascular morbidity/mortality. It is also associated with endometrial cancer when used without progestins and would not be effective in treating this patient's anovulation. Hysteroscopy (Choice C) would be useful to evaluate the uterus for structural causes of irregular menses. However, this patient's symptoms are more consistent with anovulation than with polyps or fibroids, and hysteroscopy would not be the most useful next diagnostic step. Endometrial biopsy (Choice D) is recommended when a patient presents with postmenopausal bleeding with an increased thickness of the endometrium on ultrasonography, raising concern for endometrial hyperplasia and possible carcinoma. It does not play a role in a young patient with anovulatory bleeding. Dilation and curettage (Choice E) is useful in treating heavy or abnormal uterine bleeding that does not respond to less invasive interventions, as well as for removing fetal tissue or retained products of conception. It would not be the best next step, as there are less invasive initial options. Educational Objective: Cyclic progesterone therapy is frequently used to treat anovulatory irregular menses. It functions to transition the endometrium from the proliferative to secretory phase and inhibits FSH and LH secretion to prevent ovulation. When discontinued, bleeding will occur if the anovulation is related to irregular gonadotropin release, but it will not occur if there is a structural abnormality of the uterus or estrogen deficiency. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician for a follow-up examination . Six weeks ago, a Pap smear showed low-grade intraepithelial lesions. She has had no symptoms and takes no medications . She is sexually active with one partner and uses a diaphragm for contraception . Examination shows a normal vagina , cervix , and uterus . Colposcopic examination shows an acetowhite area with punctation . The entire squamocolumnar junction cannot be visualized . A biopsy specimen of the cervix shows cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 3. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Monthly Pap smears over the next 3 months

correctExplanation: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 3 is a high-grade cervical lesion with an increased risk of progression to cervical cancer. Cervical carcinoma is classically associated with infection from human papillomavirus (HPV) high-risk strains 16, 18, 31, and 33. Risk factors include multiple sexual partners, smoking, and immunosuppression. Screening Pap smears are recommended every 3 years in women aged 21 to 29 years and every 5 years in conjunction with HPV co-testing (every three years if co-testing is not performed) in women aged 30 to 65 years. Abnormal Pap smear cytology results are most commonly evaluated by colposcopy, which allows for the visual assessment and biopsy of abnormal lesions. A colposcopy is deemed inadequate if the entirety of the squamocolumnar junction or transformation zone is not visible, as there is a possibility of undiagnosed carcinoma. In this case, the biopsy confirms CIN 3, which requires excision via a cone biopsy of the cervix (also known as cold knife conization). The cone biopsy serves to further evaluate a larger region of the cervix for cervical carcinoma and may be curative if a margin of normal cervical tissue is identified on histology. A loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) could alternatively be performed.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Monthly Pap smears over the next 3 months (Choice A) and a second colposcopy in 3 months (Choice B) would delay definitive evaluation and treatment of this patient's CIN 3 without complete visualization of the entire transformation zone, which requires excision biopsy with either a cone biopsy or LEEP. Hysteroscopy (Choice C) would allow visualization of the uterine cavity and is useful in diagnosing endometrial polyps or performing endometrial biopsies. It does not typically play a role in the diagnosis or management of cervical carcinoma. Cryotherapy of the cervix (Choice E) would be appropriate therapy for CIN 2 or 3, or for persistent CIN 1. However, it is not an appropriate therapy for CIN 3 when the entire transformation zone was not visualized because the risk of unrecognized cervical carcinoma is high. Vaginal hysterectomy (Choice F) is a potential treatment option for recurrent CIN 2 or 3, as well as cervical carcinoma. However, it is important initially to fully evaluate the entirety of the cervical transformation zone via cone biopsy. Educational Objective: CIN 3 is a high-grade cervical lesion caused most commonly by HPV high-risk strains 16, 18, 31, or 33. It portends a high risk of progression to cervical carcinoma. If the entire squamocolumnar junction is visible, appropriate management includes curative ablation or excision. However, if it is not visible, cone biopsy to evaluate the extent of the transformation zone is recommended to rule out carcinoma. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 27-year-old primigravid woman at 38 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor. She had spontaneous rupture of membranes 2 days ago. On arrival, her temperature is 39.1 °C (102.3°F). The cervix is 100% effaced and 4 cm dilated ; the vertex is at +1 station . Abdominal examination shows exquisite tenderness of the uterine fundus . Pelvic examination shows mucopurulent cervical discharge . The fetal heart rate is 180/min with good variability . Treatment with intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin is begun . Two hours after admission, the cervix remains 4 cm dilated . She undergoes cesarean delivery for arrest of active phase and delivers a healthy newborn . Six hours after delivery, the patient's temperature is 38.9°C (102°F) . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's fever?
correctExplanation: Endomyometritis is an acute polymicrobial infection of the uterine endometrium and myometrium with normal vaginal flora. Patients typically present with fever and severe tenderness of the uterine fund us. Risk factors for the development of endomyometritis include premature and prolonged rupture of membranes (greater than 18 hours), spontaneous or elective abortion, cesarean delivery, and placement of an intrauterine device. Physical examination findings include uterine tenderness on bimanual examination and mucopurulent discharge, along with fetal tachycardia on tocometry, a stress response to the maternal infection, and fever. Broad-spectrum antibiotics such as ampicillin and gentamicin are typically used to allow for appropriate coverage of the polymicrobial infection, which typically involves an array of gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria .
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Chlamydia trachomatis (Choice A) is a sexually transmitted bacterium that can cause cervicitis, urethritis, epididymitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). The clinical presentation of C. trachomatis associated PID can include fever, vaginal discharge, and pelvic organ tenderness. However, the cervical discharge in PID is typically watery, and C. trachomatis infections are not usually related to the post-partum state or prolonged rupture of membranes, which places this patient at greater risk for endomyometritis. Escherichia coli (Choice B) is the bacterium most commonly responsible for urinary tract infections. Urinary tract infections present with dysuria, frequency, urinary urgency, suprapubic tenderness, and, if the infection has ascended to the kidneys, fever and costovertebral tenderness related to pyelonephritis. Patients with urinary tract infections do not present with cervical discharge or tenderness of the uterine fund us. Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Choice C) is a sexually transmitted bacterium that can cause cervicitis, urethritis, septic arthritis, and PID. PID induced by N. gonorrhoeae can present with fever, mucopurulent cervical discharge, and pelvic organ tenderness; however, N. gonorrhoeae infections are not usually related to the post-partum state or prolonged rupture of membranes, which places this patient at greater risk for endomyometritis. Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis (Choice E) is a rare sequela of endometritis that can lead to local invasion and infection of the pelvic vein walls, which causes intimal damage and thrombosis. This condition typically presents with pelvic pain and a fever that can be widely variable in range. Diagnosis typically occurs through blood cultures. If this patient were persistently febrile despite appropriate antibiotic treatment for endometritis, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis should be considered. Educational Objective: Endomyometritis is typically a polymicrobial infection of the uterus from normal vaginal flora. In patients with postpartum fever, uterine tenderness, and pregnancy-related risk factors such as prolonged rupture of the membranes, endomyometritis should be suspected. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman , gravida 5, para 3, aborta 1, at 40 weeks' gestation is admitted in labor. Contractions began 2 hours ago . She has not had vaginal bleeding or loss of fluid. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated . Her last child was delivered vaginally at term and weighed 4300 g (9 lb 8 oz). At her last prenatal visit 1 week ago, the cervix was 50% effaced and 1 cm dilated , and the vertex was at -2 station. Examination now shows contractions that occur every 5 minutes . The cervix is 50% effaced and 6 cm dilated ; no presenting part can be felt. A fetal heart tracing shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
