choices.A: Arterial blood gas analysis of the umbilical artery

correctExplanation: Ultrasonography of the pelvis would allow the clinician to determine the fetus's positioning when no presenting fetal part can be felt at the cervical opening. Fetal malpresentation occurs when any portion of the fetus besides the occiput presents at the cervical os. This malpresentation prevents the head from properly engaging in the pelvis for descent. In some cases, excess amniotic fluid (eg, polyhydramnios) can prevent any fetal part from presenting at the cervical os until the rupture of membranes occurs. A serious complication that can occur in fetal malpresentation is umbilical cord prolapse. Because of the lack of occiput engagement at the cervical os, the cord can protrude through the cervix following the rupture of membranes before the fetus descends into the pelvis. Further contractions can cause cord compression, and the cord can be impinged by the fetus, resulting in fetal hypoxia. Given the high risk associated with vaginal deliveries in cases of fetal malpresentation, cesarean delivery may be necessary. Cord prolapse, however, is an obstetric emergency, requiring immediate cesarean delivery.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Arterial blood gas analysis of the umbilical artery {Choice A) is used to determine the oxygen levels and pH of the fetal circulation at the time of delivery. Hypoxia and acidosis can signify potentially severe hypoxic­ ischemic injury to the fetus. However, this fetus is not in distress with a normal fetal heart tracing, making an arterial blood gas analysis of the umbilical artery unnecessary. Fetal scalp stimulation {Choice B) is useful in detecting metabolic abnormalities of the fetus, including acidemia, when there are signs of fetal distress. Forceps are used to stimulate the scalp, and an elevation in the heart rate of 15/min above baseline for 15 seconds is associated with normal fetal outcome. Amniotomy {Choice D) is manual rupture of the amniotic membrane. It is frequently used to induce labor. However, it would be dangerous to perform in this patient due to the risk of cord prolapse associated with fetal malpresentation. Cesarean delivery {Choice E) is generally indicated in fetal malpresentation. However, the best next step in management is to determine the fetal position with ultrasonography, rather than move directly to cesarean delivery prior to confirmation of the fetal lie, as vaginal delivery may still be an option. Educational Objective: Rupture of membranes when there is no palpable presenting fetal body part carries a high risk of cord prolapse, which can lead to cord compression and fetal hypoxia. Ultrasonography of the pelvis allows the clinician to assess the fetal position to determine appropriate management. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 21-year-old primigravid woman at 10 weeks' gestation has had severe nausea and has been unable to keep anything in her stomach for 48 hours. She has had mild nausea and vomiting for 6 weeks . Examination shows normal findings . Ultrasonography shows a normal 10-week gestation . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Severe nausea with inability to maintain adequate oral intake is a common presenting symptom of hyperemesis gravidarum (HG) and can lead to clinically significant dehydration and starvation ketosis, which can be assessed through the measurement of urinary ketones. HG is usually associated with weight loss in early pregnancy and extends past the first trimester, when typical morning sickness resolves. Tachycardia, mild hypotension, and signs of dehydration (eg, dry mucous membranes) would be expected on vital signs and physical examination. Results of laboratory studies show ketones in the blood and urine, and depending on the degree of severity, electrolyte, volume, and acid/base abnormalities (eg, hypoosmolar hyponatremia, hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, metabolic acidosis) caused by vomiting, dehydration, ketogenesis, and severe volume contraction. As HG is commonly associated with molar pregnancy, it is also important to check a ~-human chorionic gonadotropin concentration and obtain a pelvic ultrasonography. Treatment of HG includes vitamin B6 supplementation, intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and in severe cases, total parenteral nutrition.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Complete blood count (Choice A) would not necessarily be affected by hyperemesis gravidarum or prolonged nausea and vomiting. While leukocytosis could be associated with an infectious cause of gastrointestinal distress, infection is less likely in this patient than HG given the prolonged nature of her symptoms and association with pregnancy. Volume contraction may be reflected by increased hematocrit. Measurement of serum bilirubin concentration (Choice B) would be appropriate in suspected cases of hemolysis, liver disease (eg, hepatitis), or preeclampsia, any of which could cause nausea and vomiting. For example, acute hepatitis classically presents with nausea, vomiting, jaundice, increased transaminases, and right upper quadrant pain. This patient has no reported risk factors for exposure to hepatitis, and HG is more likely. Measurement of serum glucose concentration (Choice C) may provide additional information on the adequacy of oral intake, nutritional reserves, and the possibility of gestational diabetes. However, changes in serum glucose would be nonspecific and would not establish the diagnosis. Measurement of urinary protein (Choice E) would be indicated for the evaluation of nephrotic syndrome, nephritic syndrome, and preeclampsia. Urinary ketones are more specific in HG, and urine protein is not necessarily increased. Educational Objective: Hyperemesis gravidarum presents with severe, often intractable nausea and vomiting, preventing adequate oral intake in a pregnant patient with subsequent dehydration and starvation. Associated findings include ketonuria and ketonemia, electrolyte abnormalities, acid/base disturbances, and volume contraction. Treatment consists of vitamin B6 supplementation, intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and possible total parenteral nutrition. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 37-year-old primigravid woman at 31 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She reports a 4-day history of mild difficulty breathing , especially when in the reclining position . She has no history of serious illness ; her only medication is a prenatal vitamin . Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min , respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. The fundal height is 37 cm. Pelvic examination shows no cervical dilation or effacement. Ultrasonography shows a normal-appearing fetus . The amniotic fluid index is 35 cm (N=10-20) . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Recommendation to limit dietary sodium intake
choices.E: Weekly amniocentesis for removal of fluid

correctExplanation: Polyhydramnios refers to excessive levels of amniotic fluid volume, increased uterine size relative to gestational age, and is associated with an increased risk of fetal anomalies, placental abruption, preterm labor, and postpartum uterine atony. It should be suspected when the uterine size and fundal height is larger than expected for gestational age. Polyhydramnios can be diagnosed on ultrasonography examination by measuring the amniotic fluid index (AFI). An AFI greater than 20 cm indicates an excessive amount of amniotic fluid. Polyhydramnios can be idiopathic or associated with a variety of disorders, including maternal diabetes mellitus, fetal infection with parvovirus B19, twin-twin transfusion syndrome, and fetal chromosomal or structural abnormalities (eg, esophageal or duodenal atresia, anencephaly). Fetal anomalies are the most common cause of polyhydramnios. Antenatal testing such as fetal ultrasonography with biophysical profile should be performed to evaluate for underlying fetal anomalies along with an amniocentesis to evaluate for chromosomal or genetic abnormalities if ultrasonography is nondiagnostic.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Complete bed rest (Choice A) is not recommended for patients with polyhydramnios, as this would not improve the patient's pregnancy prognosis. Further testing should be performed to evaluate the fetus for structural or chromosomal abnormalities. The recommendation to limit dietary sodium intake (Choice B) and diuretic therapy (Choice D) have no role in the treatment of polyhydramnios. Maternal sodium intake or use of diuretic therapy would have minimal to no effect on the amount of amniotic fluid, as polyhydramnios is most commonly related to underlying fetal structural or chromosomal abnormalities. Weekly amniocentesis for removal of fluid (Choice E) is performed for patients with severe polyhydramnios causing severe shortness of breath or abdominal discomfort. Weekly amniocentesis would not be appropriate in this patient with mild difficulty breathing. Educational Objective: Polyhydramnios refers to excessive levels of amniotic fluid volume and is associated with an increased risk of fetal anomalies, placental abruption, preterm labor, and postpartum uterine atony. Antenatal testing including fetal monitoring, biophysical profile, fetal ultrasonography, amniotic fluid index measurement, and amniocentesis are appropriate to assess for underlying fetal structural or genetic abnormalities. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 77-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 2, comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of intermittent episodes of vaginal bleeding . Each episode lasts 3 to 4 days and is not associated with trauma or sexual intercourse . Menopause occurred 26 years ago, and she has never received hormone therapy. Her last gynecologic examination was 38 years ago following the birth of her youngest child . She takes no medications . She has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 50 years . Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Pelvic examination shows a 2-cm , exophytic lesion on the cervix . There is no enlargement of the uterus or evidence of blood in the vagina . Results of a biopsy specimen of the lesion are most likely to show which of the following ?
correctExplanation: An exophytic lesion on the cervix is concerning for cervical cancer, which in about 70% of cases is squamous cell carcinoma derived from the epithelial lining of the ectocervix. Cervical squamous cell carcinoma begins from the transformation zone, or squamocolumnar junction, which demarcates the ectocervix and its squamous epithelium from the endocervix and its columnar epithelium. This region is the most likely initial site of cervical cancer development and is the target region of a Pap smear, a screening test for cervical neoplasia. Risk factors for cervical cancer include infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) high risk strains 16, 18, 31, or 33; early age at onset of sexual activity; tobacco use; oral contraceptive use; immunosuppression; and infection with HIV or other sexually transmitted infections. Cervical cancer classically presents with vaginal bleeding occurring with or without intercourse. It may locally invade into the bladder or rectum if advanced and can result in hydronephrosis by obstructing the distal ureteral insertion to the bladder. If distant spread occurs, the lung is a common site of metastatic disease.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Adenocarcinoma (Choice A) is a less common type of cervical cancer. Compared to squamous cell carcinoma, it makes up approximately 25% of invasive cervical cancers. In most cases, cervical adenocarcinoma and cervical squamous cell carcinoma have the same treatment. Carcinosarcoma (Choice B), or malignant mixed Miillerian tumor, is a rare neoplasm which contains components from both an epithelial and connective tissue origin. It is found in the uterus, ovaries, and fallopian tubes. Clear cell carcinoma (Choice C) is a histological variant of adenocarcinoma with a poorer response to chemotherapy. Clear cell changes may also be seen in renal and endometrial cancers. Papillary serous carcinoma (Choice D) is a rare uterine malignancy. Compared to endometrial carcinoma, it has a higher propensity for lymphatic spread. Educational Objective: An exophytic mass on the cervix is highly suggestive of cervical cancer, the most common derivation of which is squamous cell carcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma comprises 70% of cases of cervical cancer. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1, at 30 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of chronic fatigue for 2 months ; she has had a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during this period . She has had no prenatal care. She has a history of alcoholism and drug abuse . She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 59 kg (130 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m 2• She appears chronically ill. Examination shows pallor. The uterine fundal height is 28 cm. The fetal heart rate is 140/min . Laboratory studies show: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's anemia?
correctExplanation: Hemoglobin Mean corpuscular hemoglobin Mean corpuscular volume Leukocyte count Reticulocyte count Platelet count Prothrombin time Serum Bilirubin (total) ALT 6.0 g/dL 30 pg/cell 101 µm 3 4300/mm 3 0.1% 130,000/mm 3 13 sec 1.0 mg/dL 16 U/L Folic acid deficiency is a common cause of megaloblastic anemia in pregnancy because of increased folic acid requirements, especially when accompanied by malnutrition due to alcohol use disorder. Other causes of megaloblastic anemia in pregnancy include malabsorption and certain medications. In this case, the anemia is caused by impaired DNA synthesis in the red blood cell progenitor cells due to the absence of required cofactors. Symptoms include fatigue, pallor, lightheadedness, and shortness of breath. Laboratory studies will show a decreased hemoglobin concentration, increased mean corpuscular volume, decreased reticulocyte count, increased homocysteine concentration, and normal methylmalonic acid concentration. Leukocyte and platelet counts are generally normal. Peripheral blood smear will show hypersegmented neutrophils. Treatment requires folic acid supplementation and red blood cell transfusion if severe.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Bone marrow hypoplasia (Choice A) is a dysfunction of the bone marrow, leading to anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukopenia, and is typically caused by radiation or chemotherapy, toxic chemicals (eg, heavy metals), medications, autoimmune disorders, or infections. This patient's leukocyte and platelet counts are normal, making bone marrow hypoplasia unlikely. Cirrhosis (Choice B) of the liver is associated with anemia, commonly caused by chronic blood loss into the gastrointestinal tract and subsequent iron deficiency or red blood cell sequestration resulting from splenomegaly in portal hypertension. If cirrhosis is caused by alcohol use disorder, folic acid deficiency may also result. However, cirrhosis also presents with ascites, jaundice, signs of portal hypertension, and increased prothrombin time and bilirubin, none of which are noted in this case.
